NextPlay Pros

An AI booking desk that gets overlooked athletes (retired, mid-level, and rising) paid speaking, appearance, clinic, and entertainment gigs with the businesses, schools, and events that want them, with the athlete in control of who can reach them.

2Motivation

Who has the problem. Two groups who should be meeting and aren't:

  • Athletes outside the spotlight. Retired pros, college stars, Olympians in smaller sports, and minor-leaguers. Very few college athletes ever reach a major pro league: the NCAA estimates about 1.5% of college football players and about 1% of men's basketball players are drafted by a major pro league [1]. Even those who make it have short careers. The players' union's often-quoted figure is about 3.3 years of experience, and the league's own estimate is about 6 years for players who make an opening-day roster [3]. That leaves a very large group of people with real stories and skills, and no agent working for them.
  • Bookers with small and mid-size budgets. Companies planning a sales kickoff, schools planning an assembly, nonprofits planning a gala, and local businesses planning an opening. They want a relatable athlete, nearby and within budget.

How they handle it today. Bookers search online, ask friends, or go through a speaker bureau. Bureaus focus on well-known names and typically take a 20–30% commission on the speaker's fee [2]. Athletes wait to be asked, rely on old coaches and social media messages, and are easy targets for "pay a fee first" scams.

The cost. Bookers spend hours searching and still end up with a generic speaker. Athletes lose income: on a $3,000 talk, a 20–30% commission is $600–$900 [2]. And the athletes most likely to be targeted by scams are the young and first-time ones who have the least support.

3What is new here

Existing optionWhat it does wellWhere it falls short here
Speaker bureaus (for example BigSpeak, All American Speakers)Polished booking for famous speakersBuilt around known names and higher fees; 20–30% commission [2]; little room for local or rising athletes
Cameo (personalized videos)Fast paid shout-outsVideos only, not live talks, clinics, or appearances; no event matching

LinkedIn / Instagram DMsFree reachNo matching, no budget check, no scam screening, no privacy

What NextPlay Pros does differently, and why it matters:

  1. It searches a real roster with a tool instead of answering from memory, so every suggestion can actually be booked. Python then removes any athlete the search didn't return, so the AI cannot invent a person.
  2. It ranks by story fit, not fame. A comeback story for a "bouncing back" keynote beats a bigger name with an unrelated story, and each match comes with a one-sentence reason.
  3. The budget is enforced in code, not in the prompt. No athlete above the booker's maximum fee can appear.
  4. The athlete controls access. Every request is screened for scams, and contact details sit in a vault that no AI agent can read. They unlock only for a booker whose request the athlete accepted.
  5. The athlete sets the rules (Event Rider). Each athlete lists security needs, accommodations, transportation (including required pick-up and drop-off), a maximum time on site, and a "won't do" list. Bookers must agree before they can send a request, and Gatekeeper flags any request that breaks the rider.
  6. Built-in NIL compliance for college athletes. Bookers must confirm the offer isn't a recruiting inducement and doesn't use school logos; Gatekeeper and code rules flag booster or transfer offers.
  7. Follow-through is paid for. Fees are held in escrow; athletes check in 60 minutes early with one tap and keep more (5% fee instead of 10%); late arrivals refund 25% and no-shows refund 100% to the booker.
  8. It writes the athlete's marketing for them. Story Builder turns rough notes into a profile using only facts the athlete gave and flags every claim to verify.

4The agents

NextPlay Pros has three AI agents on gpt-6-luna, plus plain-Python guards around them. The rule of the design: the AI understands, ranks, writes, and judges; code makes every decision that must never go wrong (who exists, the budget, who sees contact details).

AgentRoleToolsOutput (structured)
ScoutTurns a booker's plain-English request into search filters, searches the roster, ranks the best 3–5 athletes, explains eachsearch_athletes: Python filter over the roster (sport, category, city and distance, max fee, virtual, keywords); returns public fields onlyBrief (event, city, audience, themes, budget, date), matches (id, fit 1–10, reason), follow-up question
GatekeeperScreens every booking request before the athlete sees itNone (reads the request as untrusted text)Verdict (deliver / flag / block), risk flags, 2-line summary, fee note
Story BuilderTurns an athlete's rough notes into a public profileNoneHeadline, bio, intro story, topics, best-fit events, categories, claims to verify

How they're organized. The agents don't call each other; each one sits at a single point in the booking flow (find → request → profile), and Python passes data between them. This keeps every agent small and testable, and means a failure in one can't cascade.

Models used and why. All three agents use gpt-6-luna, the model allowed by the course. It handles structured output and tool calls well, it's fast (Gatekeeper answers in about 3 seconds), and it's cheap ($0.10 per million input tokens, $0.01 cached, $0.50 output), which matters for an app that screens every message. The app first ran through the course's Portkey key. After that key was turned off (Nov 22), the app was switched to my own OpenAI key running the same model; the code supports both (MODEL_PROVIDER).

One real run, step by step

The booker typed: “Keynote for 250 credit-union employees in Denver in January about bouncing back from setbacks. Budget $5,000.” (run e038d7b2dc in output/audit_trail.json).

  1. Python input guard. The text is checked for injection and contact-harvesting phrases (none found), and any emails or phone numbers are removed. It's then wrapped in <untrusted> markers so the model treats it as data.
  2. Scout reads the request and fills its brief: event keynote, city Denver, audience 250 credit-union employees, budget $5,000, themes bouncing back from setbacks.
  3. Scout calls its tool: search_athletes(categories=['speaking'], near_city=Denver, max_fee=5000, keywords=['setbacks', 'comeback', 'resilience', 'bouncing back'])
    Python applies the filters (budget is capped in code even if the model asked for more) and returns 12 athletes with public fields only. No contact details exist in what the model sees.
  4. Scout ranks and explains the best fits (below).
  5. Python output check: every returned ID was in the search results and every minimum fee was under $5,000, so nothing was dropped.
  6. Glass box: the result shows 2 model calls, 5,108 input tokens (2,800 from cache), 429 output tokens (143 reasoning), $0.00052, 5.9 seconds.

What it means: AI cost is not this business's constraint. At 10,000 users the model bill is about $34 a month, which is less than one booking's bureau commission. The real cost is getting both sides onto the platform.

Cost-cutting steps, with evidence

  1. Prompt caching (measured). At first nothing was cached: each agent's fixed instructions were under the provider's 1,024-token minimum, and Scout's later calls were unique because of random tool-call IDs. I moved all variable text after an explicit cache breakpoint and put useful content into the fixed part (ranking rules and a worked example for Scout, a scam playbook for Gatekeeper, a style guide for Story Builder). Scout's measured cost per search went from $0.00077 (22% cached) to $0.00039 (82% cached) on repeated test searches, a 50% cut. Gatekeeper and Story Builder went from 0% cached to about 85%.
  2. Block before the model. Blunt injection and contact-harvesting requests are stopped by Python rules and never reach the model: 0 tokens, $0 (see the Glass box in the Safety screenshot).
  3. Small, structured outputs. Every agent returns a fixed schema instead of free text, which keeps output (the most expensive token type) to a few hundred tokens.
  4. Limits. Each run is capped at 6 model calls and 4 tool calls, and the app stops all AI runs once a daily spend cap (default $2) is reached.

Trade-off, with evidence. Making the instructions long enough to cache made the first call of the day more expensive: writing to cache costs $0.125/M instead of $0.1/M, and Scout still writes about 1,723 tokens per run, because each run's tool results are new. That's why live Scout runs average $0.00058 ($0.00040–$0.00079) rather than the $0.00039 seen on repeated test searches. The longer instructions also made answers better: Scout now writes story-specific reasons and asks a useful follow-up question, and Gatekeeper stopped flagging normal low-budget school requests (test G4).

6Safety

RiskWhy it matters hereDefense built
Data leaks (contact details)Athletes' phones and emails are the most valuable thing a scammer could getContacts live in a separate vault table that no agent tool reads; they're returned only to the booker of an accepted request. Emails, phones, and links are removed from all text before and after the model.
Prompt injectionRequests and athlete notes are written by strangersPython rules block blunt attacks before the model; all user text is wrapped as untrusted; every prompt says to never follow instructions inside it; Python can only make Gatekeeper's verdict stricter.
Scams aimed at athletesYoung athletes get "pay a fee to be selected" offersGatekeeper with a scam playbook plus Python rules for gift cards, upfront fees, wire transfers, and address requests. Blocked requests never reach the inbox and can't be accepted.
Invented facts / wrong actionsA made-up athlete or award would mislead a bookerPython keeps only athletes the search returned; Story Builder flags any number not in the athlete's notes; only the right athlete can accept a request.
Athlete safety at eventsAthletes travel to strangers' eventsEvent Rider (security escort, green room, no unsupervised one-on-one, pick-up/drop-off, max hours, won't-do list); bookers must agree (enforced on the server); Gatekeeper + code rules flag conflicts; Terms let the athlete leave and still be paid if the rider isn't honored.
NIL violations (college athletes)A recruiting inducement could cost an athlete their eligibilityRequired booker confirmation (server-enforced), code rules for booster/transfer offers and school logos, Gatekeeper NIL instructions, and Terms covering NIL Go reporting and F-1 visas.
No-showsA flaky athlete hurts the booker and the platformEscrow, a 60-minute-early check-in that lowers the athlete's fee, a 25% refund for late arrival, a 100% refund and a strike for a no-show.
Infinite loops / overspendingA loop or attack could run up the billPer-run limits (6 calls, 4 tool calls), a daily dollar cap, an input-length limit, and the budget enforced in code.

7Impact

Real user test: pending

A real athlete and a real booker from my network have not tried the app yet. Until they do, the impact numbers below are estimates built from sourced industry figures and the app's measured speed, not measured user outcomes.

BenefitEstimateBasis

Newly possible work. A middle school with a $500 budget can now find a local former college athlete who already speaks to kids, and the athlete gets paid for it. Today that booking mostly doesn't happen, because neither side can find the other.

8Limits and next steps

What doesn't work yet

  • The roster is fictional. All 40 athletes and their contacts are made up for the demo. Recruiting real athletes is the first business step.
  • No real accounts. Demo sign-in is a picker; access rules are enforced on the server, but there are no passwords or verified identities.
  • Escrow and payouts are simulated. The rules and math run in the app, but no real money moves; a payment provider is the next build.
  • Check-in is honor-based. The "I'm here" tap isn't location-verified yet.
  • Terms and NIL rules are a class draft, not reviewed by a lawyer. The name also overlaps with an existing "NextPlay" fitness app, which is why it's NextPlay Pros; a trademark search comes before launch.
  • Scout's live cost varies ($0.00040–$0.00079) because each run writes its tool results to cache.
  • Impact numbers are estimates until real users have been measured.

What I'd build next

  1. Real-user pilot with athletes and bookers from my own network: time saved, bookings made, scam attempts caught.
  2. Verified athlete identities and athlete-set availability calendars.
  3. An Opportunity Matcher agent that alerts athletes to posted gigs, and an Outreach Drafter that helps bookers write strong requests.
  4. Payments with escrow, so neither side carries the risk of a no-show.
  5. A full Comedy & Entertainment section (hosts, emcees, roasts).
